hello.note: Hi (high) is what most people say, to almost anyone

how-are-you.note: Often just a greeting, not a real question. Answer briefly and ask back: Good, thanks. And you?

im-well.note: I'm well is a little more formal. Then ask back: And you?

good-morning.note: Until about noon. Then good afternoon, and from about 6 pm good evening

good-night.note: Only when leaving in the evening or going to bed. To greet someone in the evening, say good evening

goodbye.note: Bye and see you are far more common. Have a nice day! is a friendly goodbye in shops

please.note: Add it to every request. English speakers use please and thank you a lot

thank-you.note: Thanks is more casual. The th is said with the tongue between the teeth

youre-welcome.note: Also: No problem, or Sure. In Britain, often No worries or Not at all

no.note: No, thank you is the polite way to turn something down

excuse-me.note: Excuse me to get past or get attention, sorry after bumping into someone. Sorry? also means pardon?

my-name.note: Also I'm... The audio uses Peter as the example name

your-name.note: The same for anyone. English has only one you

its-beautiful.note: Also: It's gorgeous! or It's amazing!

dont-understand.note: Sorry, I don't understand is softer

speak-slowly.text: Could you speak more slowly, please?
speak-slowly.say: kood yoo SPEEK mor SLOH-lee, pleez
speak-slowly.note: Could you...? is the polite way to ask for anything

speak-english.note: Useful far beyond English-speaking countries: English is the language travelers share around the world

three.note: The th is said with the tongue between the teeth

thousand.note: Written 1,000: English marks thousands with a comma and decimals with a dot, $2.50

how-much.note: Point and say How much is this? In the US, sales tax is usually added at the register, so you pay a little more than the price on the shelf

would-like.note: Short for I would like, the polite way to order. Add please. The audio uses a coffee as the example

i-want.note: Sounds blunt in English: I'd like... or Can I get...? is politer. The audio uses this one as the example

do-you-have.note: The audio uses water as the example

just-looking.note: The polite answer when a shop assistant asks Can I help you?

too-expensive.note: Softer: That's a bit more than I wanted to spend

discount.text: Can you give me a discount?
discount.say: kan yoo GIV mee a DIS-kownt
discount.note: Haggling is unusual in shops in the US, Britain or Australia. At markets and with private sellers, you can ask Is that your best price?

card.note: Cards and phone payments are accepted almost everywhere

bill.text: Can I get the check, please?
bill.say: kan eye GET tha CHEK, pleez
bill.note: The American way. In Britain and Australia, Could I have the bill, please? In the US, tip 18 to 20%

reservation.note: Add under (the name)..., such as I have a reservation under Peter

breakfast.note: Breakfast is said BREK-fast, not break-fast

toilet.note: The polite American word. In Britain, toilets or the loo; in Australia, toilets. Bathroom is fine anywhere in North America

taxi.text: Could you call me a taxi?
taxi.say: kood yoo KAWL mee a TAK-see
taxi.note: In much of the US, people use ride apps like Uber and Lyft instead

bus.note: A long-distance bus is often called a coach in Britain

bus-station.note: A bus stop is where city buses stop. Long-distance buses leave from the bus station or terminal

which-train.note: The audio uses Boston as the example

buy-ticket.text: Where can I buy a ticket?
buy-ticket.say: wair kan eye BY a TIK-et

two-tickets.note: Add one way or round trip (return in Britain). The audio uses Boston as the example

trip-length.text: How long does it take to get to...?
trip-length.say: how LONG duz it TAKE to get too ...
trip-length.note: The audio uses Boston as the example
trip-length.spoken: How long does it take to get to Boston?
trip-length.filled: How long does it take to get to ⟦Boston⟧?

allergic.note: Add the food: shellfish, nuts, peanuts, eggs, dairy, gluten. The audio uses peanuts

what-called.note: Point at the dish or item

table-for-two.note: In many US restaurants, wait to be seated: a host shows you to a table

beer.text: Could I get a beer, please?
beer.say: kood eye GET a BEER, pleez
beer.note: Draft beer is on tap. In the US you must be 21 to drink, and you may be asked for ID

coffee.note: In the US, plain coffee is filter coffee, often with free refills

tea.note: In Britain, tea comes with milk unless you ask. In the US, iced tea is common

water.note: Tap water is safe and free in restaurants in the US, Britain and Australia. Americans say the t almost like a d: WAH-der

cheers.note: In Britain and Australia, cheers also means thanks

help.note: Shout it. Emergency numbers: 911 in the US and Canada, 999 or 112 in Britain, 000 in Australia

need-doctor.note: For an ambulance, call 911 in the US and Canada, 999 or 112 in Britain, 000 in Australia

pharmacy.note: In the US, also drugstore (CVS, Walgreens); in Britain, chemist (Boots)
